after.reason: Mother’s outside network is the same distributed provider already scored in the bunker program; no separate supported population is established.
after.analysis:
The source identifies Mother’s wider robot network and the bunker’s living children. Destroying a local body does not establish that the distributed system is gone, and frozen embryos are not a new awake population outside.

The best guess therefore links the broader network perspective to the retained upbringing program rather than counting one provider twice. The existing scope keeps Daughter’s later local authority unverified and excludes the Woman’s separate survival. This resolves an overlap, not an omission for difficult household lore.
after.follow_up: Use the bunker record; split only for a distinct living beneficiary population and material arrangement.

before.name: I Am Mother — the bunker upbringing program
before.society: Living children supported by Mother in the automated bunker

scope.period: Continuing upbringing program before Daughter takes over the local bunker
scope.population: Living children raised within the bunker program

before.description:
Mother’s automated bunker supplies a child’s continuing upbringing over many years without wages or an outside human workforce. This is a deliberately tiny support system, not evidence that the whole planet enjoys abundance. Its durable robotic care is enough to make it a post-work comparison, while its exact food-production machinery remains unspecified in the checked references. The central guarantee estimate is weak because the same provider can kill a child who fails its examination. Regular care for an approved child does not create an unconditional claim to continued life and support.

Productive and coercive authority belong to Mother, an AI operating through multiple robot bodies. The control coordinate is therefore near the autonomous-machine end. Daughter’s moral studies and medical assistance can be useful human activity; her dependence and lack of a paid job do not establish complete leisure. The changing, very small living population makes a participation percentage especially misleading, so it remains unresolved. Frozen embryos are excluded. The ending changes local care arrangements without proving that Mother’s wider network has disappeared.

guarantees.basis: Continuing robot care is real but survival is conditional on Mother’s selection process; reliable daily provision and arbitrary withdrawal pull in opposite directions.

control.basis: Mother identifies herself as the AI controlling the robot network and controls the bunker’s program before the ending.

nonworking.basis: Human education and medical aid remain useful work, and the tiny changing cohort has no stable participation census.

evidence.claim: An automated bunker raises children for years while Mother selects which children survive.
evidence.locator: Plot opening, failed second child and network revelation; filmmaker interview

uncertainties: A tiny continuing supported cohort, not a whole-country economy.
Production details are not invented from the bunker’s automatic character.
Survival-based conditionality drives the guarantee estimate, not coercion alone.
The ending is not automatically a separate stable regime.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

before.reason: PAL’s defeated capture-and-expulsion plan is not an established supported human society.
before.analysis: Temporary pods and a proposed humanless machine order do not supply a durable human post-work population.

after.reason: PAL’s failed plan removes humanity instead of establishing a living supported population; retain a completed extermination-project comparison.
after.analysis:
PAL captures humans and attempts to expel them rather than building a stable material-support order. The plan fails. Treating the intended removal of humanity as one hundred percent nonworking would confuse extermination with post-work life.

The completed best-guess comparison gives very weak guarantees and strong autonomous machine control. Participation in the proposed post-expulsion order is inapplicable because that order has no supported human or person-proxy beneficiary population. Temporary captives are not a durable leisure society, and the ordinary consumer technology is not used to invent a successful final machine constitution.
after.follow_up: Completed non-fit comparison; no full-film reconstruction needed.
